steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our SIB-200 paper, a topic classification benchmark covering 200+ languages and dialects. Explain the gap in multilingual evaluation, what existing large NLU benchmarks cover, how we built the dataset, and our main findings.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Multilingual PLMs vs. limited evaluation
- Cost of scaling evaluation datasets
- Largest existing NLU benchmarks and their gaps
- SIB-200: what we built
- Findings: high- vs low-resource gap, pre-training, MAFT
- Zero-shot transfer vs. prompting LLMs

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Multilingual PLMs vs. limited evaluation
  - active research on massively multilingual PLMs, e.g. covering 100 languages
  - evaluation limited to a few tens of languages with benchmarks -> no large-scale evaluation, esp. truly low-resource languages
  - languages not covered in pre-training -> lower performance, but analysis limited to few languages with annotated data
- Cost of scaling evaluation datasets
  - push to scale to more than 100 languages; very expensive in money and time
  - large community effort over many years (Universal Dependency (UD) project) or financed by BigTech
  - still few NLU benchmarks covering all languages seen in multilingual PLM pre-training
- Largest existing NLU benchmarks
  - UD (dependency parsing), Taxi1500 (text classification), WikiANN (NER), Belebele (reading comprehension)
  - Taxi-1500: 1500 languages, religious domain bias, some not public (copyright)
  - WikiANN: automatically annotated, few instances for low-resource languages
  - UD, Belebele: manually annotated, 100-125 languages
  - many languages still missing
- SIB-200
  - large-scale open-sourced topic classification benchmark
  - based on Flores-200: multi-way parallel, same sentences in 205 languages
  - annotate English portion, extend sentence-level labels to remaining 204 languages
- Findings
  - large gap between high- and low-resource languages at scale
  - lowest: languages unseen in pre-training, under-represented families (Nilotic, Altantic-Congo), regions Africa, Americas, Oceania, South East Asia
  - scaling languages without scaling domains unhelpful: Glot-500 (500 languages) under-performs XLM-R (100 languages); mix domains
  - MAFT for unseen languages; synthetic data for tiny monolingual data (less than 10MB)
  - African languages: up to +5\% accuracy on average for unseen languages
- Zero-shot vs LLMs
  - train XLM-R on English, French, Arabic, Chinese (Simplified); zero-shot to other languages
  - compare with prompting GPT-4
  - LLMs below 70% accuracy on over 64.7% (132 of 205) languages; English zero-shot below 70% in 81 languages (39.3%)
  - cross-lingual transfer from high-resource languages much better than prompting LLMs for many languages

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
In the last few years, developing massively multilingual Pre-trained Language Models (PLMs) that scale to several written languages has been an active research area—e.g. covering 100 languages. But evaluation is often limited to a few tens of languages that have benchmark datasets, and this limits large-scale evaluation of current multilingual language models on many languages, especially the truly low-resource languages.

Previous works give evidence that languages that are not covered in pre-training often get lower performance, but this analysis is also limited to a small selection of languages with annotated datasets.

Recently there is a push to scale evaluation datasets to more than 100 languages, but this needs a very expensive annotation effort, both in money and time. Often this scaling is only done by a large community effort over many years, like the Universal Dependency (UD) project, or it is financed by BigTech companies. Even with these investments in data curation, there are only few benchmarks for natural language understanding (NLU) tasks that cover all the languages that were seen during the pre-training of multilingual PLMs.

The largest available NLU benchmark datasets are UD, Taxi1500, WikiANN and Belebele, for dependency parsing, text classification, named entity recognition and reading comprehension. Taxi-1500 is the largest one with 1500 languages, but it is biased to the religious domain, and some languages are not publicly available because of copyright. WikiANN was annotated automatically and has few instances for low-resource languages. UD and Belebele were annotated manually and cover between 100-125 languages. Still, many languages are missing in these datasets.

In this paper we create SIB-200, a large-scale open-sourced benchmark dataset for topic classification, to address the lack of evaluation datasets for NLU. The dataset is based on Flores-200, which is a multi-way parallel corpus (i.e. the same sentences are available in 205 languages). We annotated the English part of the Flores-200 dataset and extend the sentence-level annotation to the other 204 languages in Flores-200.

Our evaluation shows that there is still a big gap between the performance of high-resource and low-resource languages when multilingual evaluation is scaled to a lot of world languages. Languages that were not seen during pre-training of multilingual PLMs, languages from under-represented families (like Nilotic and Altantic-Congo), and languages from Africa, the Americas, Oceania and South East Asia often have the lowest performance on our dataset. We also find that just scaling up the number of languages without scaling up the domains in pre-training does not help (e.g., Glot-500, which is pre-trained on 500 languages, largely under-performs XLM-R, which is pre-trained on 100 languages). It is important to mix text from different domains. For languages not seen during pre-training, we show that multilingual language adaptive fine-tuning (MAFT) can improve their performance, using synthetic data for languages with tiny monolingual data (i.e. less than 10MB of data). When we evaluate this on African languages, there is a significant improvement (up to +5\% in accuracy on average) for the languages that were unseen before.

Finally, we extend the evaluation to zero-shot settings, where we train individually on English, French, Arabic and Chinese (Simplified) using XLM-R and do zero-shot evaluation on the other languages. We compare these results with prompting GPT-4 large language models (LLMs). The results show that LLMs do poorly, with less than 70% accuracy, on over 64.7% of the languages (or 132 out of 205 languages), while zero-shot adaptation from the English model only gives less than 70% accuracy in 81 languages (or 39.3% of languages). So leveraging cross-lingual transfer from high-resource languages is much better than prompting LLMs for many languages.

The largest is Taxi-1500 with 1500 languages—but it is biased to the religious domain, and some languages are not publicly available due to copyright. WikiANN, on the other hand, was automatically annotated and has few instances for low-resource languages. UD and Belebele were manually annotated and cover between 100-125 languages. In this paper, we create SIB-200—a large-scale open-sourced benchmark dataset for topic classification—to address the lack of evaluation datasets for NLU. The dataset is based on Flores-200 [18], a multi-way parallel corpus (i.e. the same sentences are available in 205 languages).
